I would not think it's sufficient to have one blanket will statement to cover all cybersecurity compliance for the system, as this is not traceable or verifiable. I understand will statements are not meant to be verifiable, but then I would argue that cybersecurity requirements should be mandatory and not 'will' statements. While I think you have the right references for policies that apply to the system, I think there should be a process to identify applicable controls and trace verifiable requirements to the system."

Create your first scenario :D

1. Create sample Git branch in the SSW-Test project

2. Under ssw-test/ums_sim/niou_fqt/ccfg, create CCFG file for SIGX_Hello_World

3. Under ssw-test/ums_sim/niou_fqt/scn/test, create SCN for SIGX_Hello_World

The scenario should accomplish the following:

a. Print out "hello world" to the terminal

b. In the UMS host.sig file, select a signal from an IP440A (discrete sensor) card. Toggle the NSIM signal to true and false and verify the USIM signal values update.

c. In the UMS host.sig file, select a signal from an IP330A (analog sensor) card. Set the NSIM signal to its min, mid, and max values and verify USIM signal values update each time.

d. In the UMS host.sig file, select a signal from an LC (LVDT sensor) card. Set the NSIM signal to its min, mid, and max values and verify USIM signal values update each time.

e. In the UMS host.sig file, select a signal from an E7_SSI (SSI sensor) card. Set the NSIM signal to its min, mid, and max values and verify USIM signal values update each time.

f. In the UMS host.sig file, select a signal from a G4 (RTD sensor) card. Set the NSIM signal to its min, mid, and max values and verify USIM signal values update each time.

g. In the UMS host.sig file, select a signal from an IP445A (discrete control) card. Set the USIM control value to true and then to false and verify the NSIM returning command matches.

h. In the UMS host.sig file, select a signal from a CMD042 (discrete control) card. Set the USIM control value to true and then to false and verify the NSIM returning command matches.

Otherwise you can't confirm nor deny your permissive signals actually are accurate if their reference is off. hmmm...
i think i've got a good idea of how to implement this harmoniously now.
will take a small amount of rework to the management code i wrote.

basic idea being, split the queue into their own respective sensor, tie them down with base card address and card ID, and signal ID.

when we iterate the cards in the GCSIM, ask the API for the list of signals tied to a card with the respective API command, then iterate the signals in that card and see if a combination of the addr, and signal ID matches my map of sensors, then take either the last message and resend it, or take the latest message, send it, and make it the last message if it was the last message in its respective queue.

this is a little different from how GCSIM currently works at a card-card basis. But i think this is the only avenue i can really take here. In a sense this shadows some of the logic from the c driver, but in a oop fashion, but in a way that makes sense in the driver.;19/Jan/26 4:57 PM;jprovenz;21600

column1: Determine SSI Clock Stimulation Via Black Box Feasibility
column10: This project is for the D440 Test team supporting SSW.
column42: In order to support Sim qual efforts, a task is warranted to determine feasibility of using the serial Black Box converter to stimulate the SSI FPGA.
column148:
1. Set up Black Box to stimulate SSI FPGA
2. Confirm or deny feasibility of this method of stimulation by using an oscope to probe the outputs of the SSI FPGA.
column178:
Posted on: Wed Nov 12 11:30:09 EST 2025
Confirmed that this is indeed working. The SSI FPGA outputs the 4 MSB bits of the SSI data message i.e. when writing x5555 55, the FPGA outputs 0101 when it receives the *4-pulse* clock (8 bits). See screenshot below for OQE. The oscope was set up with a 2V/Division vertical scale and a 20Microsecond/Division horizontal scale. The top waveform is the calculated _SSI Data (+)_ - _SSI Data (-)_ math'd signal. The bottom waveform is the calculated _SSI Clock (+)_ - _SSI Clock (-)_ math'd signal.

 

Since the oscilloscope doesn't have 4 channels, the SSI Data and SSI Clock waveforms were captured at separate times, the screenshot below transposes the SSI Data waveform onto the SSI Clock waveform screenshot. In reality, there is a small delay between the first clock pulse and the first SSI data pulse (~2 microseconds).

 

Additionally, the SSI FPGA properly holds the SSI data signal low for 25 microseconds after receiving the last clock pulse, per SSI specification.

!image-2025-11-12-11-24-35-329.png!
column271:
11/Nov/25 2:04 PM;zbutler;Have a proof of concept working. Current set up:

 
 * Using SSW-1 laptop, connected to the black box serial converter.
 * Black box serial converter is configured for DCE mode
 * Black box TX A and TX B are directly connected to IP-EP202 pins 5 and 6 (CH1 CLK + and -)
 * An oscope with 2 probes is directly connected to IP-EP202 pins 1 and 2 (CH1 DATA + and -)
 * Putty running on SSW-1 with the following config settings:
 ** Baud rate: 250,000
 ** Data bits: 8
 ** Stop bits: 1
 ** Parity: None
 ** Flow control: None
 * On the simulator, run SSI_Test_7's run.ccf and configure SSI CH1 to output data of your choice (only first 8 bits of data will be sent)
 * Once a session is established with the black box, sending a "U" results in binary 10101010, representing the 8 bit clock

 * 
 ** This results in the IP-EP202 to output the first 8 bits of data that was loaded into CH1 and can be detected and confirmed on the oscilloscope.;;;
